title: Caching and CDN
tagline: The single biggest performance win in distributed systems — understanding where data lives and how long it stays valid.

sections.content:
Most performance problems in web systems are not CPU-bound — they are **latency-bound**. A database query that takes 20ms, executed once per request, becomes catastrophic at scale: 100,000 users per second means 100,000 trips to the database every second, each round-trip burning 20ms of waiting. The server is not thinking during those 20ms — it is just waiting for the disk. **Caching** is the discipline of short-circuiting that wait by keeping a copy of the answer somewhere faster, closer, and cheaper to reach.

The word 'cache' comes from the French word for 'hiding place' — a cache is a place where you stash something valuable so you can retrieve it quickly later without having to go back to the original source. In computing, that original source might be a database on a remote server, a file on a slow disk, or an API endpoint on another continent. The cache is the local hiding place: a Redis cluster in the same data center, a CDN edge node in the same city, or a tiny in-memory dictionary in the same process.

Caches exist at every layer of the modern web stack. The CPU has L1, L2, and L3 caches measured in nanoseconds. The operating system has a page cache that holds recently accessed disk blocks in RAM. Your application has an in-process object cache. A Redis or Memcached cluster provides a shared cache across your fleet of app servers. A reverse proxy like Nginx or Varnish caches HTTP responses. A **CDN** (Content Delivery Network) caches assets on servers distributed across the globe. The user's own browser caches images, scripts, and API responses locally. Every layer trades **capacity** for **speed**: the CPU's L1 cache is 32 KB and takes 1ns; your distributed Redis cluster is 100 GB and takes 1ms; your database is 10 TB and takes 20ms.

Understanding which layer to cache in, how to express what data is cacheable and for how long, and most critically — how to keep all those caches consistent when the underlying data changes — is one of the most practical and high-value skills in systems engineering. This chapter builds that understanding from first principles.

sections.title: The Library Branch System
sections.content:
Imagine a central library warehouse on the edge of town that holds every book ever printed — millions of titles, but it takes 45 minutes to drive there and back. The city also runs neighbourhood branch libraries: smaller collections of only the most popular books, but they are a 5-minute walk away. **The CDN is your local branch library.** Popular content is replicated there so most people never have to make the long drive to the warehouse.

Now imagine the branch librarian keeps a small cart at the front desk with books that were returned in the last hour — these are the ones most likely to be requested again. **Redis is that front-desk cart.** Retrieving from the cart takes seconds; retrieving from the shelves takes minutes.

Finally, you own a small bookshelf at home with books you have read recently. You never leave the house to get those. **The browser cache is your home bookshelf.**

The librarian's hardest problem: what happens when the warehouse receives a new, corrected edition of a book? Every branch library and every home bookshelf that holds the old edition is now wrong. The librarian sends notices (invalidation), some people tear out pages and paste in corrections (update), and some people just wait until their copy is old enough that they naturally return it and pick up the new one (TTL expiry). **Cache invalidation is the library's correction problem** — and it is famously the hardest problem in computer science.

sections.title: The Cache Hierarchy: From Nanoseconds to Seconds
sections.content:
To reason about caching, you need to internalise the latency numbers at each layer. These are rough but canonical figures that experienced engineers keep in their heads:

- **CPU L1 cache**: ~1 nanosecond, ~32 KB per core
- **CPU L2 cache**: ~4 nanoseconds, ~256 KB per core
- **CPU L3 cache**: ~40 nanoseconds, ~8 MB shared
- **Main RAM**: ~100 nanoseconds, tens of GB
- **In-process object cache** (dictionary in your app): ~100 nanoseconds (no serialisation, no network)
- **Redis on the same LAN**: ~0.5–1 millisecond (one network round-trip + parsing)
- **Same-region database query**: ~1–5 ms (cached in DB buffer pool) or ~20–100 ms (disk I/O)
- **CDN edge node in same country**: ~5–20 ms
- **Origin server across continent**: ~150–300 ms
- **Cold disk I/O (spinning disk)**: ~10 ms seek + transfer

The jump from nanoseconds to milliseconds is a factor of one million. When you move from an in-process cache hit to a database miss, you are paying roughly 100,000× more latency. This is why the choice of which cache layer to use is not a micro-optimisation — it fundamentally determines whether your system can serve 10 users or 10 million users.

**Why not cache everything at the fastest layer?** Capacity and cost. Your process's heap is limited to a few GB, and data there is not shared with other processes. Redis costs money to provision and requires network overhead. Browser caches are on the user's device and cannot be purged server-side. Every cache layer has different capacity, sharing characteristics, and invalidation mechanisms.

sections.title: Caching Strategies: The Three Patterns
sections.content:
There are three canonical strategies for using a cache, and each makes different tradeoffs between simplicity, write latency, consistency, and durability.

**Cache-aside (lazy loading)** is by far the most common application-level pattern. The application manages the cache explicitly. On a read, it checks the cache first; on a miss, it queries the data source and stores the result in the cache with a TTL. On a write, it updates the data source and either deletes or updates the cache key. Cache-aside is simple because the cache is purely advisory — if it fails or is empty, the system degrades gracefully to hitting the database. The downside is the **cold start problem**: every unique key is slow on its first access, and an empty cache after a Redis restart means a traffic spike to the database.

**Write-through** caches are updated synchronously on every write. The application writes to both the cache and the database in the same operation (or the cache is an intermediary that writes through to the database). The cache is always warm for recently written data. The tradeoff: every write pays twice (cache + DB latency), and data that is written but never read wastes cache space.

**Write-back (write-behind)** writes to the cache immediately and returns success to the client, then asynchronously flushes data to the database in the background. Writes are extremely fast (just a cache write), but if the cache crashes before the flush happens, those writes are permanently lost. Write-back is appropriate for high-throughput, loss-tolerant workloads like analytics event counts or leaderboard scores, but is dangerous for financial transactions or user account data.

A fourth variant, **read-through**, is where the cache itself (rather than the application) is responsible for populating from the database on a miss. Redis does not natively support this, but caching frameworks like Ehcache do. The application always talks to the cache, which transparently fetches from the DB when needed. This moves cache logic out of application code, but the application now depends on the cache layer being available — if the cache tier is down, reads fail instead of falling back to the database.

sections.title: TTL: Time-to-Live and the Staleness Tradeoff
sections.content:
Every cache entry should have a **TTL** (Time-to-Live) — an expiry window after which the entry is automatically evicted. Without a TTL, a missed invalidation (a bug in your write path that forgets to delete a cache key) means a user sees stale data forever. With a TTL, at worst they see stale data for TTL seconds before the cache auto-expires and the next read fetches fresh data.

Choosing the right TTL is a product and engineering decision, not just a technical one. The question is: **how stale can this data be before the user or the business is harmed?**

- **Very short TTLs (1–10 seconds)**: Real-time counters, live inventory levels, stock prices. Staleness of 10 seconds is tolerable; staleness of 60 seconds is not.
- **Short TTLs (60–300 seconds)**: Search results, product listings, user news feeds. Users tolerate a few minutes of staleness in exchange for fast responses.
- **Medium TTLs (1–24 hours)**: User profile data, product descriptions, configuration. These change occasionally but not in real time.
- **Long TTLs (days to weeks)**: Reference data, country/city lists, static content not handled by content hashing. Rarely changes.
- **Effectively infinite (immutable)**: Content-addressed assets like `app.a1b2c3.js` where the URL itself changes when content changes. These can be cached forever because the URL guarantees freshness.

A key operational insight: **always set a TTL even when you are also doing explicit invalidation**. Your invalidation code will have bugs, deploys will fail, cache flushes will be missed. TTL is your safety net — it bounds the worst-case staleness window. A missed invalidation with a 5-minute TTL means 5 minutes of staleness, not permanent staleness.

Another subtlety: **staggering TTLs** prevents a thundering herd when many keys expire simultaneously. If you cache 1,000 user profiles all with TTL=3600 and they were all loaded at the same second (e.g., at server startup), they all expire at the same time, causing a simultaneous spike of 1,000 DB queries. Adding a small random jitter — `TTL = 3600 + Math.random() * 300` — spreads the expirations.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Several subtle patterns here: `redis.setex` is atomic — it sets the value AND the TTL in one Redis command, preventing the race condition where a crash between `SET` and `EXPIRE` leaves a key with no TTL. TTL jitter spreads expiration times across a window to avoid simultaneous cache misses. The write path deletes the key rather than updating it — this is simpler, avoids serialisation bugs (what if the DB row format changed?), and means the cache is populated lazily on the next read. The HTTP `stale-while-revalidate` directive tells CDNs to serve an expired entry immediately to the user while fetching fresh content in the background — eliminating the latency spike users would otherwise see on cache expiry.

sections.title: Cache Invalidation: The Hardest Problem
sections.content:
Phil Karlton's famous quip — "There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things" — has become a cliché precisely because it is so accurate. Cache invalidation is hard because it requires **distributed coordination under failure**: you need to ensure that every cache holding a stale copy of a data item is updated or evicted when the source data changes, even when networks partition, caches crash, and writes happen concurrently.

The main strategies:

**Delete on write (invalidation)**: The simplest approach. When data changes, delete all cache keys that depend on it. The next read for any deleted key will miss the cache, fetch fresh data from the DB, and repopulate the cache. This is the safest default because the usual worst case is a cache miss (slow) rather than a stale hit — though a slow reader that fetched the old row just before your write can still re-insert it after your delete, which is why a TTL is kept as a backstop. The challenge is knowing which keys to delete — if a product update affects a product detail page, a search results page, and a recommendation engine response, you need to invalidate all three.

**Update on write (write-through invalidation)**: Instead of deleting the key, update it with the new serialised value atomically. This keeps the cache warm (no cold-start spike after every write) but is harder to implement correctly — the serialised cache value must exactly match what a fresh cache-aside read would produce.

**Event-driven invalidation**: A message queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis Streams) broadcasts `ProductUpdated` events. All services that maintain a cache for products subscribe to the event and invalidate their local caches. This decouples the writer from the cache holders and is more scalable for multi-service architectures, but introduces eventual consistency — there is a window between the write and the event being processed.

**Tag-based invalidation**: Associate cache keys with tags (`product:42`, `category:electronics`). On update, invalidate all keys with a given tag. This elegantly handles the problem of one data change invalidating multiple cache entries. CDNs support this natively — Fastly's `Surrogate-Key` header, Cloudflare's `Cache-Tag`, Akamai's cache tags, Varnish via the `xkey` module — so one purge call can drop every cached page that mentions product 42. Redis does not natively support tags but they can be implemented with Redis Sets as indexes.

**Version-based invalidation**: Store a version number or timestamp with each cache key. On write, increment the version. Readers check the version before trusting a cached result. This is often used for cases where full invalidation is too expensive.

sections.title: CDN Architecture: Edge Nodes and PoPs
sections.content:
A **CDN** (Content Delivery Network) is a globally distributed fleet of caching servers. The key insight is geographic: network latency is fundamentally limited by the speed of light. Tokyo and Virginia are roughly 11,000 km apart; light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond, so one round trip costs at least ~110 ms before any routing detours or processing (real RTTs are typically 150–200 ms, and a new HTTPS connection needs several round trips). A CDN edge server in Tokyo serves that same content in 5–10ms.

CDN vendors (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, AWS CloudFront) operate **Points of Presence (PoPs)** — data centers in dozens or hundreds of cities worldwide. Each PoP contains multiple **edge nodes** (caching servers). When a user requests `https://example.com/images/hero.jpg`, the request is steered to a nearby PoP — either by DNS (the resolver gets the IP of a close PoP) or by **anycast** (every PoP announces the same IP and Internet routing delivers packets to the nearest one, as Cloudflare does). The edge node checks its cache; on a hit, it serves the asset directly. On a miss, the edge node **pulls from origin** — fetches from your actual server — and caches the response for subsequent requests from the same region.

This pulling model is called **pull-based CDN** (the alternative, push, means you upload content to the CDN ahead of time — common for large video libraries). Your origin only needs to handle the first request from each PoP for each unique cache key. **Tiered caching / origin shield** goes further: edge PoPs miss to a regional parent cache instead of to your origin, so a popular new URL causes one origin fetch instead of one per PoP. After that, the edge serves from cache until the TTL expires or you explicitly purge the edge cache.

CDNs are not just for static files anymore. Modern CDNs support:
- **API caching**: Cache `GET /api/products` at the edge with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`. The first request from any region hits origin; the next 10,000 requests in that region are served from the edge at 10ms each.
- **Edge computing**: Run JavaScript or WebAssembly at the edge node before even consulting your origin (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute). This enables personalisation, A/B testing, and auth validation at edge latency.
- **Dynamic site acceleration**: Even for uncacheable content, CDNs accelerate delivery by maintaining persistent TCP connections to your origin and routing over optimised private networks instead of the public internet.

CDNs are also your first line of **DDoS defence**. A volumetric attack that sends 100 Gbps of traffic to your domain hits CDN edge nodes — which have far more capacity than your origin — and can absorb or filter the attack before it reaches your servers.

sections.title: CDN Cache Keys, Vary, and Cache Poisoning
sections.content:
A CDN stores each response under a **cache key** — by default roughly *scheme + host + path + query string*. Two requests share a cached response only if their keys match, so the cache key decides both your hit rate and your correctness.

**Too specific a key fragments the cache.** `/products?page=1&utm_source=mail` and `/products?utm_source=ads&page=1` are different keys by default, so tracking parameters and parameter order can turn one hot object into thousands of cold ones. Fix it with CDN rules that strip marketing parameters, sort the query string, or include only an allow-list of parameters.

**Too broad a key leaks or mixes content.** If the response depends on something that is *not* in the key — a cookie, the `Accept-Language` header, the device type — the first user's version is served to everyone. The HTTP mechanism for this is `Vary`: `Vary: Accept-Encoding` (universal and safe) tells caches to keep separate gzip/brotli/plain copies. But `Vary: Cookie` or `Vary: User-Agent` usually destroys the hit rate, since nearly every request differs; CDNs instead let you add *normalised* values to the key (e.g. a device class or a single cookie such as `currency`), and personalised responses should simply be `private`.

**Cache poisoning** is the security version of the same mistake. If the origin reflects an *unkeyed* input — say, it builds absolute URLs from `X-Forwarded-Host` — an attacker sends one request with a malicious header value, the poisoned response is cached under the normal key, and every later visitor receives it. Defences: never let unkeyed headers influence a cacheable response, strip or overwrite forwarding headers at the edge, and avoid caching error pages for long.

Two more key-adjacent rules: CDNs do not cache responses that set cookies (`Set-Cookie`) or carry `Authorization` unless you explicitly allow it — good defaults to keep — and `CDN-Cache-Control` (RFC 9213) lets you give the CDN its own TTL without changing what browsers see.

sections.title: HTTP Cache Headers: The Language of Web Caching
sections.content:
The `Cache-Control` header is how your server communicates caching policy to browsers, CDNs, and proxies. It is arguably the most important HTTP header for performance engineering. Understanding its directives deeply lets you precisely control caching behaviour at every layer.

**`Cache-Control: public`** — This response may be cached by any shared cache (CDN, proxy). Use for content that is identical for all users.

**`Cache-Control: private`** — Only the end user's browser may cache this. CDNs and shared proxies must not store it. Use for authenticated or personalised content.

**`Cache-Control: no-store`** — Do not cache this response anywhere, not even the browser. Use for truly sensitive data (bank account details, medical records).

**`Cache-Control: no-cache`** — A confusingly named directive that does NOT mean 'do not cache'. It means: you may store the response, but you must revalidate it with the origin before serving it again (using `ETag` or `Last-Modified`). This adds a conditional request round-trip but avoids serving outdated content.

**`max-age=N`** — The response is considered fresh for N seconds. After N seconds, the cache considers it stale.

**`s-maxage=N`** — Like `max-age` but applies only to shared caches (CDNs). Lets you set a different TTL for CDN vs browser. E.g., `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=3600` — browsers cache for 1 minute, CDNs cache for 1 hour.

**`stale-while-revalidate=N`** — After `max-age` expires, serve the stale cached response immediately for up to N additional seconds, while asynchronously fetching a fresh copy. This eliminates the latency spike users see when a cache entry expires.

**`immutable`** — The response body will never change. Combined with a long `max-age`, browsers skip revalidation even when the user reloads the page (a forced "hard" reload still bypasses the cache). Only use with content-addressed URLs.

Practical recipes:
- **Content-hashed JS/CSS** (`app.a1b2c3.js`): `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`
- **Public API response**: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30`
- **User dashboard HTML**: `Cache-Control: no-store` (or `private, no-cache` if the browser may keep it but must revalidate)
- **CDN caches for 5 minutes, browsers always revalidate**: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=300` — do *not* add `private` here: `private` forbids shared caches from storing the response at all. (CDN-specific headers such as `CDN-Cache-Control` or `Surrogate-Control` are an alternative.)

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Notice the layering: `s-maxage` lets CDNs cache longer than browsers (`s-maxage=300` vs `max-age=60`). ETags enable conditional requests — when the browser revalidates after max-age, it sends `If-None-Match: <etag>` and the server can respond with `304 Not Modified` (no body) instead of the full response, saving bandwidth. Content-hashed files get `max-age=31536000` (one year) safely because the URL itself changes when content changes. Purge API calls are necessary after deploys that change non-hashed content.

sections.title: The Thundering Herd: Cache Stampedes and How to Prevent Them
sections.content:
Imagine a Redis key for your homepage's product listing with a TTL of 5 minutes. Your site gets 50,000 requests per minute. That is ~833 requests per second. The moment the key expires, every request that arrives while the first miss is still rebuilding the value — easily hundreds if the query takes a second — also misses, and every one of them queries the database. Your database, sized for 100 queries/second with the cache in front, suddenly receives up to 833 queries/second for an expensive query. It buckles, response times spike, and users see errors. The cache was protecting the database — now that protection is temporarily gone, and the load spike may prevent the cache from ever re-warming.

This is the **thundering herd** (also called **cache stampede**).

**Mitigation 1: Mutex / distributed lock**. When a miss occurs, only one process is allowed to query the database and repopulate the cache. All other processes wait (or serve a stale value) until the lock holder finishes. In Redis, this can be implemented with `SET lock:product_list 1 NX EX 5` (set only if not exists, with a 5-second TTL as a safety expiry). The NX (Not eXists) flag makes it atomic. Processes that fail to acquire the lock can either wait and retry, or serve the previous stale value if available.

**Mitigation 2: Stale-while-revalidate**. The CDN or caching proxy serves the stale entry to all users immediately while a background request (typically just one per cache node) fetches the fresh copy. By the time the background fetch completes, the cache is warm again. No users experience a slow response. This is built into the HTTP `stale-while-revalidate` directive and is the simplest solution for HTTP-level caching.

**Mitigation 3: Probabilistic early expiry (XFetch algorithm)**. Rather than waiting for a key to fully expire, each reader may regenerate it slightly early, with a probability that increases as the key approaches expiry and is larger for values that take longer to recompute. A key with 10 seconds remaining has a low probability of early regeneration; a key with 1 second remaining has a high probability. This amortises the regeneration cost across many requests, preventing the simultaneous miss.

**Mitigation 4: Background refresh pattern**. A separate background worker continuously refreshes hot cache keys a few seconds before they expire, completely decoupled from the request path. The request always finds a warm cache. This is ideal for keys that are always needed (e.g., homepage data, global configuration).

**Mitigation 5: TTL jitter**. When pre-warming many keys simultaneously (e.g., at startup), add random jitter to each key's TTL. Instead of all 10,000 user profiles expiring at T+3600, they expire between T+3400 and T+3800. This spreads the miss load across 400 seconds rather than concentrating it at one moment.

flowchart TD
  A["Key expires"] --> B["1000 concurrent requests\nall get cache MISS"]
  B --> C{"Mutex acquired?"}
  C -->|"YES: 1 request"| D["Query DB\nrepopulate cache"]
  C -->|"NO: 999 requests"| E["Serve stale value\nor wait for lock"]
  D --> F["Cache warm again"]
  E --> F
sections.caption: Mutex pattern for thundering herd prevention. Only the request that wins the distributed lock queries the database. All others serve the previous stale value immediately. After the lock holder repopulates the cache, all future requests hit the cache again.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `SET key value NX EX N` Redis command is the canonical distributed mutex primitive: it sets the key only if it does not exist (NX = Not eXists), with an expiry (EX) as a safety net in case the lock holder crashes. Waiters poll the cache for a bounded time instead of all falling through. XFetch stores, next to the value, how long it took to compute (`delta`) and its logical expiry; each read refreshes early when `now + delta × β × (−ln rand)` passes that expiry. Far from expiry this almost never fires; close to it, one of the many readers recomputes before the key actually disappears — no lock and no background worker needed. `β > 1` refreshes earlier, `β < 1` later.

sections.title: Cache Eviction Policies: What Gets Dropped When the Cache is Full
sections.content:
A cache has finite memory. When it is full and a new item needs to be stored, something must be evicted. The **eviction policy** determines what gets dropped. Redis supports several policies, configured via `maxmemory-policy`:

**LRU (Least Recently Used)** — evict the entry that was accessed least recently. The intuition: if you have not used something in a long time, you probably will not need it soon. Redis's `allkeys-lru` evicts any key; `volatile-lru` only evicts keys that have a TTL set.

**LFU (Least Frequently Used)** — evict the entry that has been accessed the fewest times. Better than LRU for workloads with a mix of hot and cold data: under LRU, a burst of one-off keys (a crawler, a batch scan) can push out keys that are read thousands of times an hour but happened not to be touched in the last few seconds; LFU keeps the frequently used ones. Redis approximates LFU with a small logarithmic counter per key that decays over time, so formerly popular keys eventually lose their protection.

**Random** — evict a random key. Simple, predictable performance overhead, but suboptimal hit rate.

**No eviction (the default)** — return an error when the cache is full. This is suitable when Redis is used as a primary data store rather than a cache. As a cache, this policy is almost always wrong.

For application caches, `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu` are the most common choices. LFU is generally better for cases with highly skewed access patterns (20% of keys serve 80% of traffic — the classic Pareto distribution of web workloads). LRU is simpler and works well when recency is the best predictor of future access.

**Cache capacity planning**: web access patterns are usually heavily skewed (roughly Zipf-distributed), so a cache holding a small fraction of all keys can serve most requests. You do not need to cache everything — you need to cache the hot portion. Measure it: track hit rate against cache size (and eviction counts) and grow the cache until extra memory stops buying meaningful hit rate.

**Historical context**: The concept of CPU caching dates to the 1960s. IBM introduced the first hardware cache in the IBM System/360 Model 85 in 1968. Web-scale caching as we know it was pioneered by Akamai, founded in 1998 as a CDN born out of Tim Berners-Lee's challenge at MIT to 'solve the Internet's infrastructure problems'. Redis was created by Salvatore Sanfilippo in 2009, initially to scale LLOOGG, his real-time web log analyser. Memcached, the other dominant in-memory cache, was created by Brad Fitzpatrick at LiveJournal in 2003 to handle the site's database load as it scaled. Much of today's web caching practice grew out of the 2000s scaling stories of sites such as LiveJournal, Facebook, and YouTube.

**Common mistakes and interview insights:**

**Mistake: caching without a TTL.** `redis.set(key, value)` with no expiry means the entry lives until explicitly deleted or Redis is flushed. One missed invalidation creates stale data forever.

**Mistake: caching mutable per-user data at the CDN.** Setting `Cache-Control: public` on `/api/user/dashboard` will cause the CDN to serve one user's private data to another user. Always use `private` or `no-store` for personalised responses.

**Mistake: an unplanned CDN cache key.** Tracking parameters fragment the cache; headers or cookies that change the response but are not in the key serve the wrong variant to everyone (and enable cache poisoning). Decide what goes into the key deliberately.

**Mistake: not testing the cache-miss path.** Developers test with a warm cache and never see the miss path. In production, a Redis restart or first deploy creates a cold cache. The miss path must handle gracefully.

**Interview insight: 'What is cache invalidation?'** Answer: the process of removing or updating stale cached entries when the source data changes. Explain the three strategies (delete on write, update on write, TTL expiry) and why TTL is a safety net even when you also invalidate explicitly.

**Interview insight: 'What is a CDN and how does it work?'** Answer: globally distributed fleet of caching servers at Points of Presence. DNS routes users to the nearest edge node. Edges pull from origin on miss, then cache based on response `Cache-Control` headers. Describe the latency savings (200ms → 10ms) and the pull model.

items: **Caches form a hierarchy from nanoseconds to milliseconds**: CPU L1/L2/L3 → RAM → in-process cache → Redis → CDN edge → database. Each layer is slower but larger and more shared. Satisfying requests at a higher layer cuts latency by orders of magnitude.

**Three core caching strategies**: cache-aside (app manages cache on reads and writes — most common), write-through (cache updated synchronously on every write — always warm), write-back (write to cache, flush async — fastest writes but durability risk). Choose based on your read/write ratio and staleness tolerance.

**Always set a TTL** — even when you have explicit invalidation. TTL is your safety net: a missed invalidation becomes bounded staleness (TTL seconds) instead of permanent staleness. Add jitter to TTLs set in batch to prevent simultaneous expiry stampedes.

**Cache-Control headers are the interface between your server and the caching infrastructure.** Know the key directives: `public` vs `private`, `max-age` vs `s-maxage`, `no-store` vs `no-cache`, `stale-while-revalidate`, and `immutable`. Content-hashed files can be cached for a year; personalised responses should use `private` or `no-store`.

**CDN edge caching** reduces latency from 200ms (cross-continent) to 5ms (nearby edge node) for static assets and cacheable API responses. CDNs also absorb DDoS attacks, offload bandwidth from origin, and — with edge computing — can personalise content without hitting your origin at all.

**CDN cache keys** (default: host + path + query) decide hit rate and correctness: strip tracking params, use `Vary: Accept-Encoding` but avoid `Vary: Cookie`, keep personalised responses `private`, and never let unkeyed headers change a cacheable response (cache poisoning).

**Cache invalidation** is the hardest part: keeping caches consistent when source data changes. The safest strategy is delete-on-write (cache key is deleted after DB update; next read repopulates it fresh). More advanced approaches include event-driven invalidation via a message bus and tag-based invalidation for CDNs.

**Thundering herd** (cache stampede) occurs when a popular key expires and many concurrent requests simultaneously miss the cache. Mitigate with a distributed mutex lock (Redis `SET NX EX`), `stale-while-revalidate`, or probabilistic early expiry (XFetch). Always test your cache-miss path — it is what users see after deploys and Redis restarts.

quiz.question: In the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern, what happens on a cache miss?
options: The application queries the database and stores the result in the cache with a TTL
The load balancer retries the request on a different cache node
The request returns a 503 error until the cache is manually warmed
The cache automatically fetches from the database without any application code
quiz.explanation: Cache-aside puts cache management in the application. On a miss the app queries the DB directly, writes the fresh result into the cache with a TTL, and returns the data to the caller. Future requests for the same key hit the cache. The cache is advisory — if it fails, the system gracefully falls back to the DB.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between write-through and write-back caching?
options: Write-through uses TTL expiry; write-back uses explicit invalidation
Write-through updates both cache and DB synchronously; write-back writes to cache immediately and flushes to DB asynchronously
Write-through only caches read results; write-back only caches write results
Write-through is used for CDNs; write-back is used for in-process caches
quiz.explanation: Write-through keeps the cache consistent by updating it synchronously with every DB write (both succeed before returning to the caller). Write-back writes only to the cache immediately (low latency) and defers the DB flush to a background process — at the risk of data loss if the cache crashes before flushing.

quiz.question: A CDN-cached product page has a terrible hit rate. Logs show the same page requested as /p/42?utm_source=mail, /p/42?utm_source=ads&ref=x, and so on. What is the best fix?
options: Add Vary: User-Agent so each browser gets its own optimised copy
Lower max-age so the CDN refreshes the page more often
Switch the response to Cache-Control: private
Configure the CDN cache key to ignore (or allow-list) query parameters that do not change the response
quiz.explanation: By default the query string is part of the CDN cache key, so every tracking-parameter combination becomes a separate, mostly cold cache entry. Excluding parameters that do not affect the response (or including only an allow-list) collapses them back into one hot entry. Vary: User-Agent would fragment the cache even further, a shorter max-age reduces hits, and private disables CDN caching altogether.

quiz.question: What does the `stale-while-revalidate=30` directive in a Cache-Control header tell a CDN or browser?
options: Reject all requests for 30 seconds after the max-age expires
After max-age expires, serve the stale cached response immediately for up to 30 seconds while fetching a fresh copy in the background
Revalidate the cached response every 30 seconds using ETag headers
Delay serving the response by 30 seconds to allow the cache to warm up
quiz.explanation: stale-while-revalidate lets the cache serve a slightly stale response immediately (avoiding the latency of an origin round-trip) while simultaneously fetching fresh content in the background. The stale content is served during revalidation, so users never experience the latency spike that would occur if the cache simply expired and forced an origin fetch.

quiz.question: What is the 'thundering herd' (cache stampede) problem?
options: Many concurrent requests simultaneously missing the cache when a popular key expires and all hitting the database at once
A cache that grows too large and evicts useful entries too aggressively
A CDN that accidentally caches private user data and serves it to other users
Write-back cache losing data because the background flush worker cannot keep up
quiz.explanation: When a hot cache key expires, all concurrent requests get a cache miss at the same moment and simultaneously query the database. The DB, which was sized for low load thanks to the cache, receives a sudden massive spike that can cause it to buckle. The cache was providing protection — when it briefly disappears at key expiry, the full load hits the DB. Mitigations include distributed mutex locks, stale-while-revalidate, and TTL jitter.

quiz.question: Which Cache-Control header is correct for a content-hashed JavaScript file (e.g., `app.a1b2c3d4.js`)?
options: Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: private, max-age=60
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Cache-Control: no-cache, must-revalidate
quiz.explanation: A content-hashed filename includes a hash of the file's contents in the URL. When content changes, the URL changes — so browsers and CDNs always request the correct version. This makes it completely safe to cache for a year (31536000 seconds). The `immutable` directive tells browsers not to revalidate even on a hard refresh, eliminating unnecessary conditional requests.

quiz.question: A CDN serves users with low latency primarily by:
options: Compressing database query results before forwarding to app servers
Encrypting assets at the network layer to reduce TLS handshake time
Load balancing write traffic across multiple database replicas
Caching content at geographically distributed edge nodes close to end users
quiz.explanation: CDN edge nodes are located in data centers worldwide. A user in Tokyo is served from a nearby Tokyo edge node at ~5-10ms rather than an origin server across the Pacific at ~200ms. The CDN caches content on first pull from origin, so all subsequent requests from that region are served at edge latency. Physical distance and the speed of light are the fundamental constraints CDNs address.

quiz.question: What does `Cache-Control: private` tell a CDN edge node?
options: Cache this response and encrypt it before storing at the edge
Cache this response only for users with a valid authentication token
Do not store this response — it may only be cached by the end user's browser
Store the response for 60 seconds then require revalidation
quiz.explanation: `private` means the response is specific to one user and must not be stored in any shared cache (CDNs, proxies). Only the end user's own browser may cache it. Using `public` on personalised content is a critical security mistake — the CDN could serve one user's private data to a different user who requests the same URL.

quiz.question: Redis's `allkeys-lfu` eviction policy evicts which key when the cache is full?
options: The key with the shortest remaining TTL
The key that was accessed least recently
The key with the lowest access frequency, tracked by a counter that decays over time
A randomly selected key regardless of access pattern
quiz.explanation: LFU (Least Frequently Used) evicts the key with the lowest access frequency. Redis approximates it with a small logarithmic counter per key that decays over time, so it reflects recent popularity rather than all-time totals. This beats LRU for skewed workloads: a key read thousands of times an hour but not in the last few seconds survives a burst of one-off keys that would push it out under LRU.

quiz.question: You want to add a TTL jitter to prevent thundering herd on mass cache population. Which implementation is correct?
options: Set all keys with the same TTL but different key names
Add a random value within ±10% of the base TTL to each key's expiry
Set TTL to zero and rely on explicit invalidation only
Use LRU eviction so Redis naturally staggers expirations
quiz.explanation: Jitter adds randomness to TTL values, spreading expiry events over time rather than concentrating them at a single moment. For example, with a base TTL of 3600 seconds and 10% jitter, keys expire between 3240 and 3960 seconds — a 720-second window instead of a single instant. This prevents all keys set at startup from expiring simultaneously and causing a mass cache miss. LRU eviction addresses memory pressure, not expiry timing.
